facts.summary: Alabama has no state overtime statute, so the federal FLSA rule (time-and-a-half after 40 hours per week) governs; there is no state daily overtime or higher salary floor.
facts.citation: No Alabama statute; FLSA 29 U.S.C. 207 applies
facts.notes: Alabama has enacted no wage-and-hour overtime law; wage/hour enforcement is handled federally by the U.S. DOL Wage and Hour Division. Verify no new state OT statute each cycle.

facts.summary: Alabama has not enacted a state minimum wage, so the federal minimum wage of $7.25/hour applies statewide.
facts.citation: No Alabama minimum wage statute; FLSA 29 U.S.C. 206 applies
facts.notes: No state minimum wage law as of July 2026. SB171 (2026) proposed a $10.00 state minimum wage effective 2027 but had not been enacted as of this check; re-verify in future cycles.

facts.summary: The Alabama Uniform Minimum Wage and Right to Work Act bars any county or municipality from requiring employers to pay a wage or provide benefits beyond what state or federal law requires, voiding local minimum wage ordinances.
facts.notes: This is an Alabama-specific addition (preemption) rather than a difference in the wage rate itself; enacted 2016 in response to a Birmingham local ordinance.

facts.value: no additional classes beyond federal (age covered by separate state statute)
facts.summary: Alabama has no general state fair-employment statute adding protected classes; race, color, religion, sex, national origin, and disability claims rely on federal Title VII and the ADA, while age is separately protected by state law.
facts.citation: No general Alabama anti-discrimination statute; see Ala. Code 25-1-20 et seq. for age
facts.notes: Alabama does not have a broad state FEPA; the only stand-alone state employment-discrimination statute is the age law. No state additions for sexual orientation/gender identity, etc.

facts.value: no general state law; age statute covers employers with 20+ employees
facts.summary: Alabama has no general state anti-discrimination statute, so Title VII/ADA (15+ employees) govern most claims; the state Age Discrimination law applies only to employers with 20 or more employees, matching the federal ADEA.
facts.notes: Alabama does not lower the federal 15-employee threshold; the only state coverage threshold is 20 employees for age claims, the same as the federal ADEA.

facts.summary: The Alabama Age Discrimination in Employment Act prohibits employment discrimination against persons age 40 and older by employers with 20 or more employees, providing a state cause of action parallel to the federal ADEA.
facts.notes: AADEA mirrors federal ADEA coverage (age 40+, 20+ employees) but adds a state-court remedy. Statute spans sections 25-1-20 through 25-1-29.

facts.value: 180 days (state age claim); no state FEPA otherwise
facts.summary: A state-court age-discrimination action under the AADEA must generally be brought within 180 days of the alleged discriminatory act; Alabama has no state fair-employment agency, so other discrimination claims follow the federal EEOC deadlines (180/300 days).
facts.notes: 180-day AADEA limitation drawn from secondary summaries citing Ala. Code 25-1-29; confirm exact limitation period and any EEOC-dismissal 90-day follow-on against primary statutory text before relying on it. Alabama has no state FEPA, so Title VII/ADA claims use EEOC's 180/300-day windows.

facts.summary: Alabama's State Employees Protection Act prohibits supervisors from retaliating against state employees who report violations of law, rule, or regulation to a public body; it does not cover private-sector employees.
facts.notes: Protection is limited to state government employees. Alabama is a strict at-will state and courts do not recognize a general public-policy wrongful-discharge tort for private employees; private whistleblowers rely on federal statutes.

facts.summary: Alabama has no dedicated wage-payment statute, so unpaid-wage claims are pursued as breach of contract, with a six-year limitations period for written contracts and three years for open or unwritten accounts.
facts.notes: These are the general contract statutes of limitations applied to wage claims because Alabama has no specific wage-claim statute or administrative wage-claim process; the applicable period depends on how the claim is characterized. Federal FLSA claims have their own 2/3-year limits.

facts.value: no state law; next regular payday (federal default)
facts.summary: Alabama has no statute setting a deadline for final wages after separation, so the FLSA default (payment by the next regular payday) applies, and payout of unused leave depends on employer policy or contract.
facts.citation: No Alabama final-pay statute; FLSA applies
facts.notes: No state timing requirement for final paychecks and no state mandate to pay out accrued vacation absent a policy or contract.
